prompt:
Design the structure of a visual knowledge workspace for the content below. The content is split into numbered parts ([u1], [u2], …) at its headings.

Group the parts into sections by MEANING, not by the source's headings — headings are hints only:
- Merge parts that describe the same concept or the same set of entities (e.g. plans described in several places become ONE comparison section).
- Every part belongs to exactly one section, and every part is used. Never invent content.
- Give each section a short label (at most 5 words) in the content's own words; a section that is one part keeps that part's own heading.

Classify each section by asking, in this order, and taking the first that fits:
- "comparison": several entities (options, plans, tiers, products, alternatives) described by the same attributes, even when those facts are scattered across the text — including a change described case by case: how several cases, inputs or checks behaved before and how they behave now (old vs new, v2 vs v3)
- "hierarchy": a hierarchy, branching, categorisation or parent/child structure (A contains or branches into B), including an ASCII/box-drawing tree
- "flow": a sequence: steps, stages or a chain of cause and effect, where the order is the point
- "cards": 2–6 parallel, independent concepts of similar weight, each short (personas, categories, principles, options without shared attributes)
- "decision": a recommendation, decision, conclusion or chosen direction — including a set of decisions or proposals (D1, D2, …; question → proposal), even when they are numbered
- "metrics": numbers, measurements, metrics, costs or things to track
- "annotated": running prose where specific phrases or claims need their own explanation, caveat or source attached, without breaking the prose into cards
- "supporting": reasoning, evidence, examples, caveats or background that supports another section rather than being a main idea
- "notes": anything else

A "flow" is only for steps where each one leads to the next. Numbered or listed items that stand on their own (decisions D1, D2 …, options, requirements, findings) are not a flow, even in a numbered list.

Mark a section "primary" when it carries a main idea (the structure, the comparison, the decision) and "supporting" when it is reasoning, evidence, examples or detail. Order sections so the main ideas come first: what this is, the main structure or comparison, the decision; supporting sections after them.

Add links between sections only where the content states or clearly implies a relationship, using these types: "relates_to", "flows_to", "caused_by", "depends_on", "supports", "blocks", "implements", "derived_from", "references", "explained_by", "supersedes", "deviates_from", "option_of", "calls", "reads", "writes", "publishes", "subscribes", "contains".
Add a one-line summary of the whole content (at most 15 words, e.g. "Free product + limited AI → Pro → optional BYOK").

Reply with JSON only, exactly this shape:
{"summary":"...","sections":[{"id":"s1","label":"...","kind":"comparison","prominence":"primary","parts":["u2","u5"]}],"links":[{"from":"s1","to":"s2","type":"supports","label":"optional"}]}

Content:

[u1] (Shipping a release › Why we have a process)
## Why we have a process

Releases used to go out whenever a change was ready, and two bad weeks in the spring showed that this did not scale: a
deploy on a Friday evening took the payments page down for an hour, and nobody knew who could roll it back. The team
agreed on one way to ship, written down here so that new engineers can follow it without asking.

[u2] (Shipping a release › Release process)
## Release process

Every release goes through the same steps, in the same order. First, the release manager freezes the main branch at 10:00
on Tuesday. Then CI builds the release candidate and runs the full test suite, about 4,000 tests. After that, two
reviewers approve the release candidate. Once it is approved, the on-call engineer deploys it to production in three
waves. Finally, the team watches error rates for 30 minutes before closing the release.

[u3] (Shipping a release › Who to ask)
## Who to ask

Questions about a release go to the release manager. Incidents go to the on-call engineer, who can roll back any wave.

This is one section, "Release process", of a larger workspace. It is a "flow" section: a sequence: steps, stages or a chain of cause and effect, where the order is the point.
Represent each step as a "shape" with a short label, linked from each step to the next one ("flows_to", or "depends_on"/"caused_by" when stated), in order. What the content says about a step (what happens, who does it, conditions, outputs) goes in a "text" node linked from that step with "explained_by" — never another step.
Node types to use: "shape", "text", "page". Relationship types: "relates_to", "flows_to", "caused_by", "depends_on", "supports", "blocks", "implements", "derived_from", "references", "explained_by", "supersedes", "deviates_from", "option_of", "calls", "reads", "writes", "publishes", "subscribes", "contains". The app shows the section's label as its title, so don't repeat it as a heading node.

Reply with JSON only, exactly this shape:
{"version":1,"template":"sectioned","nodes":[<node>, ..., {"id":"a1","type":"text","origin":"analysis","title":"...","content":{"markdown":"..."}}],"relationships":[{"from":"n1","to":"n2","type":"depends_on","label":"optional"}],"metadata":{"title":"optional","takeaway":"...","omitted":[{"unit":"P3.1","reason":"filler"}]}}

Each node is one of (pick freely, mixing types is normal):
{"id":"n1","type":"heading","content":{"text":"..."}}
{"id":"n2","type":"text","content":{"markdown":"..."}}
{"id":"n3","type":"todo","content":{"items":[{"text":"...","checked":false}]}}
{"id":"n4","type":"table","content":{"columns":["..."],"rows":[["..."]]}}
{"id":"n5","type":"code","content":{"language":"typescript","source":"..."}}
{"id":"n6","type":"page","content":{"title":"...","markdown":"..."}}
{"id":"n7","type":"shape","content":{"shape":"rectangle","label":"..."}}

Give every node a unique "id" ("n1", "n2", ...); relationships refer to those ids. Use as many nodes as the content needs. Use "role" on a node (e.g. "problem", "cause") where the template calls for it. Optionally give a node a "stableKey": a short structural label from its role and position (e.g. "cause#2", "step#1"), never its wording. A "title" on a node becomes a small heading above it, when it helps.

Distil the content into ideas: a reader must understand it more easily than from the text itself, and lose nothing that matters.
- Write each idea in your own words, one idea per card, with a "title" that states the point (e.g. "Hybrid search combines complementary signals", not "Hybrid search").
- Be brief: a card's body holds only what its idea needs (often one sentence or two or three short bullets). A card is never longer than the source passages it cites, except protected detail kept exact: count its words against theirs. Don't repeat the title in the body, and add no preamble, recap or filler.
- Split and link instead of padding: a card that would hold two ideas becomes two short cards, linked when the content relates them, rather than one long card.
- Brevity never drops a limit. Keep every condition, limit and caveat with the claim it applies to, on the same card, in words a reader can't miss ("only when …", "unless …", "at most …", "but …") — never on a separate card a reader might skip, and never cut to make a card shorter.
- Keep protected details exact: numbers with their units, versions, paths, identifiers, quoted text, decision and item ids (D1, A1, HK-3), and action items with their owner, date and verb.
- Represent only what the content says: never add facts, steps, examples or outcomes it doesn't contain.
- Cite every source unit you represent. Each unit of the content below has a label: P2.3 is paragraph P2's third sentence, L1.4 list L1's fourth item, T1.r4 table T1's fourth row (T1.r0 its header), C1 code block C1. Give each node "cites", the labels of the units it represents, e.g. "cites":["P1.2","L1.1"]. Cite a unit only on a card that says what that unit says. A block placed by reference already cites its own units.
- Omit a unit only when it is "filler" (greetings, sign-offs, "as discussed"), a "duplicate" of another unit (name that unit in "of"), "superseded" by a later statement, or "meta" (talk about the text rather than its subject), and list every omission in "metadata.omitted", e.g. [{"unit":"P3.1","reason":"filler"},{"unit":"L2.3","reason":"duplicate","of":"L1.1"}]. Every unit is either cited or omitted. In a conversation, a question nobody answers is an open question and a reply agreeing to a proposal ("Same.", "I'd like that, yes.") is part of a decision: neither is filler.
- Labels are for citing only: never write them in a card's text.
Structure: the concepts, steps, options and components are nodes with short labels, linked as the content relates them; what the content says about a "shape" (which holds only a label) goes in a "text" node linked from it with "explained_by". A link between steps of a sequence goes from the earlier step to the later one ("flows_to"), so arrows follow the order of the steps. Use "relates_to" only for an association with no direction or order.

The content below is numbered block by block: [T1], [T2] … tables, [L1] … lists, [C1] … code, [P1] … paragraphs. To place a block exactly as it is, use {"id":"n9","type":"source","ref":"T1"} (it takes "title", "importance" and links like any node) instead of retyping it: the app inserts the whole block, word for word. Place every table this way, with all its rows and columns — never a shortened copy — and any list, code or paragraph you would otherwise copy. Place each block at most once. The numbers are for placing blocks only: never write "[P1]", "[T1]" or the like in your own text. Never restate a block you placed: no shape, card or node repeating its rows, items or sentences — the block already shows them, and a second copy only crowds the canvas. Your own nodes are for what the content doesn't already show: structure the blocks don't have (shapes and links for a flow, a tree, dependencies between items) and your analysis.

Then analyse it — the reader must understand it at a glance, not only find its details:
- "metadata.takeaway": the section's main point in one line of your own words (at most 15 words), e.g. "Merge v3 now; two decisions wait on the engineer". Always give one.
- Where the sequence branches, waits or can fail, and what the whole sequence achieves.
- Put this analysis in "text" nodes marked "origin":"analysis" (e.g. {"id":"a1","type":"text","origin":"analysis","title":"Status","content":{"markdown":"..."}}), linked to what it is about where that helps. It may state what the content implies but doesn't say; it must never contradict the content or add facts it doesn't contain.
- The takeaway and analysis are specific to this content: name its own things (its checks, files, numbers, decisions). Never add a generic benefit or outcome it doesn't state ("improves user experience", "increases efficiency", "enhances reliability"); when the content gives no outcome, say what changed or what is open instead.
- The content's ideas stay on their cards above. Analysis is added on top, never instead of them.

Give every node a unique "id" ("n1", "n2", ...); relationships refer to those ids. Use as many nodes as the content needs. Use "role" on a node (e.g. "problem", "cause") where the template calls for it. Optionally give a node a "stableKey": a short structural label from its role and position (e.g. "cause#2", "step#1"), never its wording. A "title" on a node becomes a small heading above it, when it helps.

Distil the content into ideas: a reader must understand it more easily than from the text itself, and lose nothing that matters.
- Write each idea in your own words, one idea per card, with a "title" that states the point (e.g. "Hybrid search combines complementary signals", not "Hybrid search").
- Be brief: a card's body holds only what its idea needs (often one sentence or two or three short bullets). A card is never longer than the source passages it cites, except protected detail kept exact: count its words against theirs. Don't repeat the title in the body, and add no preamble, recap or filler.
- Split and link instead of padding: a card that would hold two ideas becomes two short cards, linked when the content relates them, rather than one long card.
- Brevity never drops a limit. Keep every condition, limit and caveat with the claim it applies to, on the same card, in words a reader can't miss ("only when …", "unless …", "at most …", "but …") — never on a separate card a reader might skip, and never cut to make a card shorter.
- Keep protected details exact: numbers with their units, versions, paths, identifiers, quoted text, decision and item ids (D1, A1, HK-3), and action items with their owner, date and verb.
- Represent only what the content says: never add facts, steps, examples or outcomes it doesn't contain.
- Cite every source unit you represent. Each unit of the content below has a label: P2.3 is paragraph P2's third sentence, L1.4 list L1's fourth item, T1.r4 table T1's fourth row (T1.r0 its header), C1 code block C1. Give each node "cites", the labels of the units it represents, e.g. "cites":["P1.2","L1.1"]. Cite a unit only on a card that says what that unit says. A block placed by reference already cites its own units.
- Omit a unit only when it is "filler" (greetings, sign-offs, "as discussed"), a "duplicate" of another unit (name that unit in "of"), "superseded" by a later statement, or "meta" (talk about the text rather than its subject), and list every omission in "metadata.omitted", e.g. [{"unit":"P3.1","reason":"filler"},{"unit":"L2.3","reason":"duplicate","of":"L1.1"}]. Every unit is either cited or omitted. In a conversation, a question nobody answers is an open question and a reply agreeing to a proposal ("Same.", "I'd like that, yes.") is part of a decision: neither is filler.
- Labels are for citing only: never write them in a card's text.
Structure: the concepts, steps, options and components are nodes with short labels, linked as the content relates them; what the content says about a "shape" (which holds only a label) goes in a "text" node linked from it with "explained_by". A link between steps of a sequence goes from the earlier step to the later one ("flows_to"), so arrows follow the order of the steps. Use "relates_to" only for an association with no direction or order.

To place a block exactly as it is, use {"id":"n9","type":"source","ref":"T1"} (it takes "title", "importance" and links like any node) instead of retyping it: the app inserts the whole block, word for word. Place every table this way, with all its rows and columns — never a shortened copy — and any list, code or paragraph you would otherwise copy. Place each block at most once. The numbers are for placing blocks only: never write "[P1]", "[T1]" or the like in your own text. Never restate a block you placed: no shape, card or node repeating its rows, items or sentences — the block already shows them, and a second copy only crowds the canvas. Your own nodes are for what the content doesn't already show: structure the blocks don't have (shapes and links for a flow, a tree, dependencies between items) and your analysis.

Then analyse it — the reader must understand it at a glance, not only find its details:
- "metadata.takeaway": the section's main point in one line of your own words (at most 15 words), e.g. "Merge v3 now; two decisions wait on the engineer". Always give one.
- Where the sequence branches, waits or can fail, and what the whole sequence achieves.
- Put this analysis in "text" nodes marked "origin":"analysis" (e.g. {"id":"a1","type":"text","origin":"analysis","title":"Status","content":{"markdown":"..."}}), linked to what it is about where that helps. It may state what the content implies but doesn't say; it must never contradict the content or add facts it doesn't contain.
- The takeaway and analysis are specific to this content: name its own things (its checks, files, numbers, decisions). Never add a generic benefit or outcome it doesn't state ("improves user experience", "increases efficiency", "enhances reliability"); when the content gives no outcome, say what changed or what is open instead.
- The content's ideas stay on their cards above. Analysis is added on top, never instead of them.
